chunks: When you need multiple scope channels. The question: When would I need multiple scope channels?
A scope with several channels shows how signals relate to each other in time.
Two or four channels tell you which signal moved first, how much later the other followed, and by how much. Most hardware bugs are about exactly that kind of cause and effect.
A detective with one witness hears one story. With four witnesses who each noted the time, the detective builds a timeline and sees who saw what first.
All channels of a scope share one clock, so they are witnesses on the same timeline. One catch: probes and cables of different lengths add different delays.
Four channels give you the power-up order at a glance. Compare the gaps between enable and each rail and the PG assertion with the sequencing rule in the datasheet.
A single channel would give you only one of these rows and none of the ordering.
Channel: one input on the scope, with its own probe and vertical scale. Trigger on the symptom: starting the capture when the problem appears, such as a reset line falling.
Pre-trigger history: samples recorded before the trigger, so you can see what led up to it.
Shared ground: all channels' ground connections are tied together inside the scope, so every probe ground must go to the same voltage.
Skew: a timing offset between channels caused by different cable or probe delays. Math channel: a computed trace such as CH1 minus CH2, or CH1 times CH2.
A microcontroller resets at random. You connect the reset line to channel 1 and the supply rail to channel 2.
Trigger on the reset line falling, in single mode, with the trigger point near the right side of the screen. The screen then shows mostly history.
If the rail dipped just before the reset, the cause is power. If it is clean, look elsewhere. For timing, a signal travels about 5 nanoseconds per meter of cable.
Two cables that differ by 30 cm are 1. 5 nanoseconds apart, enough to spoil a 2 nanoseconds measurement. That is the whole idea.
"I use multiple channels whenever the debug question is about how signals relate in time.
For example trigger on a reset on one channel and watch the supply on another to see if it drooped first.
They're also used for sequencing several rails, delay between clock and data, multi-wire buses like SPI, and math like volts times amps for power.
I watch for shared grounds, probe skew, and that some scopes drop sample rate when more channels are on."
Quick check. Your board resets randomly. Which setup best shows whether the supply drooped first?
